lesson_title: Johannesburg to Cape Town in Three Moves
hook_text: Ruler, multiply, unit. That is how a geographer gets from Johannesburg to Cape Town without leaving the classroom.
clip_script: Here is a map of South Africa at one to ten million. Knock five zeros off that number and you know one centimetre stands for a hundred kilometres. Ruler from the middle of Johannesburg to the middle of Cape Town: 12,6 centimetres. Multiply by a hundred: 1 260 kilometres in a straight line. But nobody drives in a straight line. The N1 bends around mountains and through towns, about 1 400 kilometres. Straight line, use a ruler. Along the road, use string and follow the bends. And for a trip across the world? A flat world map stretches the Earth like flattened orange peel, so the honest answer comes from a globe and a piece of string pulled tight. That tight string is the shortest route, and it is the route aeroplanes fly.
visual_style: A whiteboard outline of South Africa, a ruler snapping from Johannesburg to Cape Town, then a string tracing the N1; finally a globe with a taut string arcing between two cities.
mood: Road-trip energy with a smart twist.
pacing: Fast calculation, a pause on the bendy road, a final turn to the globe.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and measure any trip on any map.
